content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to use task-relevant “hints” to conduct test-time adaptation to combat distribution shifts. In addition to directly optimizing the main network, the authors also propose using a side network to generate parameters on-the-fly as a faster alternative, taking these “hints” as input. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on several geometric and semantic tasks and benchmarks. The authors also provide interesting analyses to help readers better understand the method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**
1. The authors conduct experiments on many tasks and benchmarks, and the proposed method shows promising results.
2. The authors provide detailed analysis to help readers better understand the method.

**Weakness**
1. Unrealistic assumption and setting.
- In my opinion, the so-called “hints” are actually sparse or weak labels, which are rarely available at inference time. Optimizing using ground truth labels will of course do a better job than optimizing with proxies because we are evaluating with ground truth!
- For monocular depth estimation, the authors assume that we have a batch of images from the same scene to compute structure-from-motion, which is a strict constraint. This means we cannot use this method if we want to adapt our model to one single image suffering unknown corruption. If you say one image is not enough to estimate distribution shifts, then we also cannot adapt the model to a batch of images coming from different scenes but containing the same type of distribution shift, which is a reasonable setting. On the other hand, what if SfM fails under certain types of shifts or scenes (e.g., environments without rich textures to do feature matching)? Such “hints” are not always possible to obtain.
- For semantic segmentation, why can we assume we have sparse ground truth annotations for each class? This does not make sense to me. I think this is not a test-time adaptation setting but more like an interactive segmentation problem with human input. Of course, the authors can argue that we can select confident or likely correct predictions from the pre-trained model to use as pseudo labels. But I did not see such experiments. I don’t think we can assume an oracle model or human labels exist at test time.
- Similarly, for image classification, why can we assume the weak labels will exist at test time? I don’t think we should assume there is an oracle model or human to provide these weak labels. 
- 3D reconstruction and optical flow estimation may be the only tasks with realistic assumptions since we need at least 2 images from the same scene (which you can use SfM or multi-view stereo to get matching points). However, the scope of this paper in this case will become much more narrow, and the authors need to make significant updates to this submission.

2. Method
- Once we have sparse ground truth or weak labels, TTO in this paper becomes trivial. Both episodic and online settings have been studied in test-time adaptation works such as TTT and TENT. Also, instead of a simple L1 loss, there are extensive studies on robust loss to optimize these geometric or semantic tasks. For example, the scale-invariant loss for depth estimation [A1].
- Thus, the only technical contribution is the proposed RNA. However, the authors do not provide enough details about this method. For example, I don’t know what the network architecture is and how this side network handles the input. 
- If RNA only takes “hints” as input, then why can RNA regress the parameters to handle distribution shift? “Hints” are sparse ground truths or weak labels, containing no information about the shift.
- If RNA takes both “hints” and initial model prediction as input, then how are they combined? Also, as the authors mention, RNA has never been exposed to any shifts, then why is RNA more robust to unseen shifts than the main task network?
- Does RNA-Scratch also take both “hints” and initial model prediction as input?

3. Unfair setting and lack of comparisons.
- For test-time adaptation methods, why is TENT (with entropy minimization) the only baseline? First, TENT is mainly designed for classification but not regression tasks. I don’t think entropy minimization is a reasonable objective for test-time adaptation. Second, there are many follow-up works proposed using better objectives (e.g., [A2][A3], etc.), and the authors also mention and discuss some of them in the related work section. Then why are they not included in the result section?
- I think distributionally robust approaches should also be compared. Otherwise, how do we justify the advantage of the test-time adaptation method over these robust methods? For example, we should at least show that test-time adaptation outperforms distributionally robust approaches in some cases or some shifts.

4. Presentation.
- The method description is not clear enough. A lot of details are missing.
- The authors refer to the appendix too many times. The main manuscript should be self-contained without referring to the appendix.
- Instead of showing so many tasks and results in the main manuscript, the authors should instead focus on one or two and try to convey the message clearly. 

**Reference**
- [A1] Ranftl et al. Towards Robust Monocular Depth Estimation: Mixing Datasets for Zero-Shot Cross-Dataset Transfer. TPAMI 2022
- [A2] Gandelsman et al. Test-time training with masked autoencoders. NeurIPS 2022
- [A3] Liu et al. TTT++: When does self-supervised test-time training fail or thrive? NeurIPS 2021
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The presentation is not good. The main manuscript is not self-contained. A lot of details are missing.

Quality: Not good enough for ICLR.

Novelty: Technical novelty is limited. The RNA component seems interesting, but there is not enough details or experiments to study it thoroughly.
content.summary_of_the_review:
There are several fatal weaknesses in this paper. First, the assumption is not realistic at all, at least for most of the tasks presented in this paper. I don’t know how other settings/tasks can learn from this paper. Second, the authors try to show too many tasks and results in the main manuscript, while not providing enough details to elaborate on the method. Last, not comparing to strong baselines or state-of-the-art methods.

In my opinion, there are two orthogonal themes in this paper: “hints” and RNA. Assuming the availability of “hints” at test time is not realistic at all. Unless the authors have a way to estimate these “hints” using initial model prediction instead of an oracle or a human, I would suggest the authors drop this component. I can see some preliminary results of RNA with existing supervision signals instead of “hints”. This part is good and should be discussed and studied more in the main manuscript instead of the appendix.

In summary, I would suggest the authors rethink the scope of this paper, make modifications according to the reviews, and resubmit it to the next venue.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces an adaption Rapid Network Adaptation (RNA) for adapting neural networks to distribution shifts at test time. The primary idea is to leverage proper adaptation objectives based on the target task related properties, called Hints (task-aware proxies). Experiments show consistent improvements over the baselines on diverse tasks, datasets, and distribution shifts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strengths] 
+ This paper is well-written and easy to follow. 
+ There are a lot of qualitative and quantitative results included in the manuscript.

[Weaknesses] 
- The solution formulation is somewhat unreasonable. For example, the model, including test-time optimization (TTO) and rapid network adaption (RNA) to be adapted, relies on ground truth supervision. The ground truth supervision, namely the so-called Hints. However, existing test-time adaption as [A] may be supervised by pseudo labels or simulated results rather than the ground truth. It is not reasonable to retrieve the ground truth annotations for test-time optimization unless the handled tasks concerning human-machine interaction, such as interactive segmentation.

Related paper:
[A] Dian Chen, Dequan Wang, Trevor Darrell, Sayna Ebrahimi: Contrastive Test-Time Adaptation. CVPR 2022: 295-305
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well-written and easy to follow, yet the assumption is not reasonable.
content.summary_of_the_review: It has been shown that models trained with inadequate supervision can perform similarly to those trained with perfect supervision, as shown in the section on weak supervision for semantic tasks. However, the reviewer does not understand that ground truth supervision used for test-time model adaption is reasonable. In most training scenarios, ground truth supervision is only allowed in the training-time phase rather than the testing-time phase.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focus on test time adaptation (TTA) across different tasks like monocular depth, dense 3D reconstructions, semantic segmentation and image classification. Authors emphasize that task aware losses are crucial and helpful for TTA, rather than proxy losses like entropy minimization. Towards the task aware losses, authors use weak ground-truth supervision. In particular, small percentage of labelled pixels for dense tasks and coarse labels for image classification. Authors show that using such weak supervision improves TTA. In addition, authors propose to use a proxy network (Rapid Network Adaptation – RNA) to assist TTA. The RNA trained to regress the network adaptation parameters on TTA samples, supporting to reduce the computational effort during test-time.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. Paper is clearly written, easy to understand the concepts. 
2. Shown that the task aware losses with weak supervision improves performance. 
3. Proposed RNA networks reduces the computation effort.

Weakness:

My major concerns like on author assumptions that “hints are readily available during test time” and they specifically refer to ground-truth information (in the form of weak supervision). In particular, small percentage of pixels for depth, labelling few pixels for semantic segmentation and using coarse labels for ImageNet. It is important to note that this information is not readily available during test time that require human annotations. This concern questions the significance and applicability of this paper on TTA. Using ground-truth supervision as hints limits practicality of the approach. Further more, the concept of using proxy network during TTA has introduced in AuxAdapt (see below reference), which is not discussed in the paper. Some of the other relevant papers are missing the discussion in the related work.

[a1] AuxAdapt: Stable and Efficient Test-Time Adaptation for Temporally Consistent Video Semantic Segmentation

[a2] Efficient Test-Time Model Adaptation without Forgetting

[a3] Test-Time Adaptation to Distribution Shifts by Confidence Maximization and Input Transformation 

[a4] Continual Test-Time Domain Adaptation

[a5] MM-TTA: Multi-Modal Test-Time Adaptation for 3D Semantic Segmentation

[a6] On the Road to Online Adaptation for Semantic Image Segmentation

content.title: Withdrawal of Our Submission
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their feedback. We provide a brief comment below, mainly to disambiguate and position, which clarifies what we intended from this paper. The main points of this paper are: 

- __A method for test-time adaptation.__ We proposed RNA, which involves training a side-network to use test-time information for adaptation of a main network. This network acts akin to a “controller” and adapts the main network based on a feedback signal. Furthermore, we showed that it can _generalize to unseen shifts_, and as it only requires a forward pass at test-time, it is _fast_. This aspect of the paper was found promising based on the reviewers comments. 
- __Test-time objectives (hints).__ The reviewers’ concerns were regarding this aspect. In particular, the assumption of having access to click annotations and coarse labels. We agree that the current disposition is unclear, as the primary intent of the paper was to use some adaptation signal for executing RNA, rather than fixating on developing new adaptation signals. We chose to use simplified signals (e.g. course labels, clicks, etc) that are accessible and quantifiable in the real work to demonstrate the concept works on different hints. The necessary details to understand when and why such hints make sense and are not an unreasonable choice are not clear in the current write up (e.g. sparse depth resembles the depth from a radar sensor which can be indeed used for adapting a vision-based dense depth estimator). We agree that this part should be revised, thus, we wish to withdraw the current draft.
